hints: Muscle cells are normal diploid body cells with 64 chromosomes, so ask yourself what has already happened to the DNA in S phase just before early prophase starts.
Remember 1 chromatid equals 1 DNA molecule, and in telophase the two new sets of chromosomes are still inside one shared cell until cytokinesis finishes.
walkthrough:
**Start with the normal chromosome number**

Great start, let's get our bearings. A muscle cell is a diploid somatic cell, so its normal number is 64 chromosomes and 64 DNA molecules in G1.

Before mitosis, S phase of interphase copies every DNA molecule.

**Count DNA in early prophase**

In early prophase, DNA replication is finished. Each of the 64 chromosomes now consists of two sister chromatids, and each chromatid is one DNA molecule.

Key calculation:
$$64 \text{ chromosomes} \times 2 \text{ DNA per chromosome} = 128 \text{ DNA molecules}$$

**Count DNA in telophase of the same cell**

This is the clever part. In anaphase the sister chromatids separate, so now we have 64 single-chromatid chromosomes at each pole. But telophase happens before cytokinesis is complete, so both sets are still counted as being in one cell.

Key calculation:
$$64 + 64 = 128 \text{ DNA molecules per cell}$$
So the answer is 128 in early prophase and 128 in telophase.

options.A: Incorrect, as it forgets DNA replication. 64 in prophase would mean no replication, and 32 in telophase incorrectly halves the DNA as in meiosis.
options.B: Incorrect, as 64 in prophase ignores that each chromosome has two chromatids (two DNA molecules) after S phase.
options.C: Correct, as early prophase has 64 x 2 = 128 DNA molecules, and the whole telophase cell still contains both daughter sets (64 + 64 = 128) before cytokinesis.
options.D: A tempting trap. 128 is right for prophase, but 64 is the count per new nucleus in telophase, not per whole cell which still holds 128.
